subject: english-language
title: Martha's Vineyard to MLE
welcome_lead: Islands and inner cities — from Labov's Vineyard to Multicultural London English, watch identity drive change.
meta_desc: Labov Martha's Vineyard, MLE, dialect levelling and Cheshire et al. at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have followed variation from island fishers to London teenagers — identity remains its engine.

concepts.def: Labov's 1963 study of /aɪ/ and /aʊ/ on the Massachusetts island; centralisation marked island identity against summer tourists.
A youth variety described by Cheshire, Kerswill, Fox and Torgersen (2011) in multi-ethnic London, with features from Jamaican, South Asian and Cockney sources.
Reduction of distinctive regional features under mobility, mass media and contact (Kerswill).
The formation of a new variety from contact between dialects (e.g. Milton Keynes new town speech).

walkthroughs.body_html:
On Martha's Vineyard, Labov found older fishermen centralising the diphthongs /aɪ/ and /aʊ/. Younger islanders who wanted to remain on the island adopted the same feature.

The change indexed local identity against the seasonal tourist influx — variation as resistance.

Cheshire, Kerswill, Fox and Torgersen's 2011 'Linguistic Innovators' study mapped MLE features: fronted GOOSE, the quotative this is me, new pronoun man.

Crucially, inter-ethnic friendship groups, not single ethnic backgrounds, drove the innovations — a London-wide youth identity.

Kerswill argues dialect levelling reflects mobility and media exposure: regional features are abandoned in favour of supra-local norms.

Estuary English in the South-East shows levelled features that span the region — neither RP nor strict Cockney.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between overt and covert prestige?
options: Overt prestige is the high status of standard varieties recognised by society (RP, Standard English); covert prestige is the hidden status of non-standard varieties within particular groups, signalling solidarity or toughness.
Only standard language has prestige; non-standard varieties have none.
Overt prestige is loud speech and covert prestige is quiet speech.
Labov showed that everyone speaks the same way regardless of background.

mcqs.q: What does Labov's research show about language variation?
options: Overt prestige is loud speech and covert prestige is quiet speech.
Labov showed that everyone speaks the same way regardless of background.
Labov showed that working-class people speak ungrammatically.
Language varies systematically by social class, gender, age and context — and speakers shift style depending on formality, often unconsciously.
Alternating between languages or varieties within a conversation or even a single utterance — often patterned by context, topic, identity or audience. Code-switching is rule-governed, not random.
Overt prestige is loud speech and covert prestige is quiet speech.
Code-switching means using slang words in formal speech.
Code-switching shows the speaker doesn't know either language properly.
